reviews.review: Great game, makes you think, and is the most realistic hacking game I've played.

I really love this game. Hacknet provides a really "legitimate-feeling" hacking experience, despite actual hacking being much different. It is satisfying when you are able to solve a problem creatively. You can find many new machines apart from the main storyline to hack. It is quite an relief when you just barely block a trace by the skin of your teeth, and quite a dissapointment when a trace falls through...
All of these reasons can turn into great experiences, I would definitely recommend this game to anyone that can enjoy using their brain for games... Instead of just aimlessly shooting people (not trying to criticize FPS games, I can enjoy them from time to time too)

Amazing game. Definitely feels like a long-due spiritual successor to Uplink. Improves on it in a lot of ways, too; for example, by requiring the player to use a command-line interface rather than just clicking and dragging widgets around. It's also really fun and the soundtrack is pretty bitchin'.

Okay, now for the criticisms.

First, the game is way too easy and straightforward. Hacking every system can essentially be boiled down into three steps: take down firewall/proxy, open ports, run magical hacking tool. Missions are similarly straightforward: once you Hack into the Mainframe™ you dig around for clues, and if that fails, use your magical scan tool. Sometimes you're on a timer. And so on.

Second, missions are way too linear and the progression is kinda bugged. You are automatically assigned one mission at any given moment, and canceling it breaks the game by preventing you from proceeding to the next story-important mission. Some missions, e.g. the /el sidequest line, don't even trigger unless you meet some very specific criteria, and you can't backtrack to it later on. And even on the final set of missions, you can't even complete it unless you track down one very specific piece of software from a specific quest line which may or may not be available to you before the story-critical mission is forced upon you.

Third, a lot of hacking is just waiting for your damn magical programs to crack open ports and passwords for you after typing stuff into the command line. Which is boring, especially considering there usually isn't much of a challenge to begin with.

Anyway it's still a good game and I have zero regrets about throwing money at it.
As a Computer Scientist this is suprisingly realistic. The commands are acutal Linux and the methods used are real. Actually, that's not cool; that's scary....

I'm coming to this game from Uplink. That being said I didn't really enjoy Uplink. The smallish UI and strange "hacking" mechanics in it don't seem as intese as a hacker game should. 

Hacknet fixes those problems. Most of the hacking you do requires typing like "gamey" hacking, but simple enough for a person like me to understand and enjoy. Most of the game seems like a puzzle, you have to figure out which commands do what in order to get into the computer. 

Sometimes the game suprises me with its authenticity. For example typing OpenCDTray into the terminal actually opens your tray. Another example is how when you get a trace started on you, the timer will tick to zero. When that happens it bluescreens your game (not the PC) and restarts the game. It really is a beautiful game for that reason.

It's like Uplink, with slightly less content, but a LOT more fluid.

10/10 Would open my CD Tray again.

This is basically Uplink 2.0, only with less GUI and more command line interfacing. For all those who enjoy an intricately unraveling story, rewarding puzzles and terminal screens. Plus, the soundtrack is excellent!

Today, I bought a steam gift card to buy this game and as soon as I played it, I really liked the game; however, I made a huge mistake with a mission and the worst part was that I couldn't redo.  As a result, I asked for a refund.  To be honest, I'm going to just wait for a more patched and complete game before I buy this again, if I ever do.

reviews.review: I can finaly "hack the planet" with this game! Very addicting.

I really loved this game. Hacknet provides a really legitimate-feeling hacking experience. It is satisfying when you solve a problem creatively. It is intriguing when you find new machines to hack. It is exhilarating when you just barely block a trace by the skin of your teeth. For that I commend this game.

However, there is a small but significant issue regarding the contracts system that I want everyone to be aware of. First, know that, in the game, you can only work on one contract at a time. I'm not sure why this is, but I believe the developers have said they are releasing a patch to allow for multiple contracts. Not sure when, though.

In the current version of the game, you can choose to abandon contracts of you want to try out a different one. That's all well and good, but here the thing: You cannot complete any contracts you abandon. At all. *POOF* They're gone! Here's the kicker: this includes story missions. 

I got stuck on a story mission and thought that there would be some program I needed to get from a side mission. I abandoned the story mission to pursue other contracts, thinking, "They surely wouldn't lock me out of the story missions." They would. And they did. So now, I have to make a new game and start eight hours of work all over again. 

Despite the whole novel of complaining I've thrown at you, I do really like this game. I do. Which makes it all the more frustrating when I encounter game-breaking and strangely arbitrary game design choices such as the abandon contract feature. Just take my warning before you play.

Hacknet is perfect for those who like classics like Uplink. The UI flow is fantastic and easy to use, the missions allow progression and learning new things, and the missions are even randomized to some degree to allow replayability. The only downside so far is that when you get late into the game there are some game breaking bugs that stop you from progressing. I solved this by finding an IP of a server in my save file in order to get a program that I needed. The developer of the game has made it perfectly that they know of this bug and are working on it. You might want to wait off on this game until that's fixed, if such things bother you. The only downside to this game is a major flaw. The flaw being no rewards system at all for hacking. You can't earn money from missions to upgrade your machine or anything. All that exists is story progression. So if you care nothing about Bit and his story, this game will be extremely boring to you. So if you think you'll find the hacking repetative and you care nothing about Bit, I'd give this game a pass.

TL;DR Really fun game, but needs some work. Should have released into early access with the state that it's in.

UPDATE - A couple of days after I post this review, the developer announces that he patched the bug that made the game impossible to complete. While another bug does exist at present (where if you do not accept the Junebug mission in time, you lose the opportunity to continue with the main story), it is possible to work around this by reloading an old save.

Upon reaching the end of the game, I am absolutely convinced that this game is one of (if not) the best hacking simulators on the market. The final mission in the game is so intense. I had to do it in several parts and my heart was racing each time I started it. There was nothing I could suggest to make the gameplay itself any better. Maybe adding in more missions to give it some replayability and a bit more freedom to go off and hack to your hearts content for good or for evil. However, that could be a DLC pack and can easily be added in. As the game stands, it deserves an 8/10, purely because it's still not perfect in terms of the bugs. However, they should be fixed soon given the dedication the dev has with this game.

- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -

Let me be perfectly clear with this before you read any further. I LOVE Hacknet. It's a fantastic game and is definitely better than Uplink by a mile. The use of real computer commands makes it feel much more realistic and the storyline is pretty awesome to boot. Plus, the time limit you have when a trace counter starts rapidly going down and you're waiting for the password crack to finish so you can intercept the trace creates one heck of an adrenaline rush.

However I cannot recommend it as it is now. There is a single bug I have encountered that makes the game impossible to complete. I will try to avoid giving away any spoilers, so this will be a bit vague. Later in game you are required to take on a mission that is part of the main storyline. However, you do not choose when this mission comes to you. It is automatically sent to you in an email and I'm not 100% sure what the criteria is for it appearing. To complete it, you need an .exe file used to crack a specific port which is only available by taking on a side mission. However, this mission is locked and once again, I do not know what the criteria is to unlock it. So I tried to take on the other available missions in an attempt to unlock the one I needed. In order to do this, you must abort the main storyline mission. Aborting a mission means you can NEVER attempt it again, making it impossible to continue with the main storyline. While I discovered it is possible to obtain the .exe without the mission, following an online walkthrough to obtain the information needed to get it instead of getting it in game feels wrong on so many levels, especially since it's deeply hidden within this seemingly permanently locked mission.

So at this time, I can't recommend it. The game is good, but I haven't been able to finish it because of this bug. The developer seems to be quite willing to take feedback and work on it so if you're reading this, I eagerly await a patch for this game. I can't wait to finish it.

Overview:
  Hacknet is at its heart a digital exploration game. Using a powerful suite of programs that you gain throughout the game, the player must gain access to systems and perform contracts. The game has a very similar feeling to the older game Uplink and hacking is done through speed, knowledge of your tools, and system resource management (RAM).

Plot:
  The plot is pretty threadbare, but does a good job of pulling the overarching story together. The ending makes sense, but is a little lacklustre for the scope of what you supposedly accomplish. However, this is in character for hacking since public attention is bad for those at the fringe of legality. Overall, I enjoyed the plot, but the beginning intro and ending are really the only interesting points. It's difficult to do characterization when all you have is text, but I felt that more effort could have been put into letting the player get to know more of the other people in the story (naix, maybe some backstory on bit, etc.)
 
Gameplay:
  The gameplay is separated into two parts: hacking and forensics. The actual hacking is rather easy since most trace timers last far more than long enough and some systems actually keep your admin after you disconnect. The main challenge in this format is simply knowing which order to run the port hacking programs in so that you can maximize efficiency and minimize time spent not logged in. These do get quite intense at times and a few conflict sequences definitely run the point home that you're not invulnerable. Progress through the game is blocked in a sort of metroid-vania way, in the sense that you need this power to unlock that type of port to enter. I enjoyed this, but wished that there were more early systems that you needed to backtrack to.

  That backtracking is part of the second part of the gameplay, the forensics. By this I mean that you spend your time going through file systems trying to spot the file with the password, scanning computers to reach connected nodes, and searching for new IPs to check out. In fact, there is an entirely alternative gameplay path that is only reached with diligent use of your tools. I loved the exploring, but it did feel quite limited, or at the very least truncated to be more accessable for players who might not be used to the gameplay style.
  Part of the joy of the exploration comes from the humor that you find in random files. From a script for "Titanic 2" that involves the icebergs running onto land and attacking people to Bash.org IRC logs, there is a decent amount of silliness and joy to discover. However, since the files in the systems you hack are procedurally generated, more content would have been nice. There's only so many times that you can see the same Bash log before you stop wanting 
to check them out because you feel you've seen everything.

Pros:
*really fun
*sense of satisfaction from difficult hacks
*humor: From a mission where you need to write "d*cks" on the main webpage of "Nortron Security" to an homage to *chans (the secret /el/ image board), the game is very funny and self aware.
*exploration
*failure penalty fair
*short: Hacknet doesn't wear out its welcome, which it probably would have for some players by the end game.

Cons:
*repetitive
*short
*not enough content
*exploration feels like it was stunted for ease of access

Hopes:
*mods:
	I feel that mods could make this from a good game to a great game. I'd love to try my hand at adding new features to the game.
*hardware changes
	Uplink let the player purchase hardware upgrades to increase ram or processing power as well as giving access to more complicated systems. Hacknet's only customization for your computer is changing the display theme.
*more story
	Getting to know the other hackers more personally would be very enjoyable.
*higher difficulty
	clearing the logs on a system means that they won't track you down - but this presents a problem. You always leave a disconnect log, but the game doesn't notice that a disconnect log without a matching connect log implies
	that the IP that disconnected was responsible for the attack. Having to selectively clear logs and/or bounce IP like Uplink might be a good idea. In addition, I would have enjoyed more difficult forensics and encrypted files
	that you can't find the password for. I was a little miffed a few times when I spent some time looking through the files to find the next IP when all I had to do was type "scan". More threats to the player as well as uncertainty
	in how well you performed the attack would be welcome.
*more challenges
	Maybe adding in new network architecture requiring the player to do a different minigame than typing the first two letters of a program and tab completing.
*multiplayer
	multiplayer is hinted at being in development in the files on the endgame server.

Bottom Line:
I love this game and want to spend so much more time on it, but sadly it seems that there's no more content. This type of game is sadly lacking in today's market and is quite unique. It pulls off what it does well and with much better guidance than Uplink. You should try it if you're interested in learning basic cmd/*nix commands and command line navigation/use while having fun, if you like tech and silly games, or if you're a fan of Uplink.

As of the current version (3.010), there are a pile of game breaking bugs which haven't been fixed, including save file issues with the cloud, missions not being unlocked or being started before you have the means to finish them, and not being able to continue under certain conditions.  There are no real fixes yet, and people have resorted to save file hacking to try and get around some of the worst ones (and even that doesn't always work).  I'm not convinced it's even possible to finish the game w/o cheating or save hacking in its current state.

If you still want to buy it, then you NEED to treat this as an Early Access Beta and watch the forums closely for updates.  Otherwise, save your money, and wait for a stable release.

[b][h1]I almost wanted to write this as a negative review.[/h1][/b]
However, on balance, I switched the direction of that thumb.

Full disclosure: I am a professional sysadmin, and I Tux and I are old buddies. He didn't like me at first, but I pulled his source and patched it, and now he [b]loves[/b] me. 

[h1] First the things that drove me up the wall...[/h1]

Mostly, it was the [b]almost[/b] unix commands, like 'RM *' instead of 'rm -r -f' and things like supporting tab completion and wildcards but [i]not[/i] partial names [i]with[/i] wildcards. I can't tell you how many times muscle memory had me type 'RM @32[Tab]*' to delete all logs that began with @3213 - but this does [i]not[/i] work in-game. You either delete everything, or have to type in each file one at a time. Fortunately, this ultimately proved irrelevant after I later discovered all other in-game admins use their keyboards only as a protective drool mat for their desks (more on that below.)

Also, the fact that you could just RM * and expect that the sysadmin on the system wouldnot find it suspicious at all that the system lacks logs of any kind for a whole time perod, and the last log is a x.x.x.x disconnected with no matching 'connected' message. Nope. Nothing suspicious there.

Almost makes me ashamed of wearing a white hat in real life. 

[h1]Kudos to the devs to for trying to acquaint us with RFC1700, but...[/h1]

What I found silly and pointless was to use real port numbers that you'd exepct to see in real life servers (22 for ssh, etc) but making you type in the port numbers for your magic 'sploit to work against (where there is never any deviation [i][b]ever[/b][/i] from the standard) is just silly as well.

[i]Note: I guess the IANA in-game must have been OK with that company creating the protocol that uses port 104, as that is in the range of ports they control assignments for... Just sayin' [/i]

I would assume a hacker as talented as 'bit' that could write a magic rootkit could figure out that if I didn't provide a port number for an SSH exploit, that it should just assume something as reasonable as, oh... assuming that the ssh daemon is running on port 22 like every. single. system. in the game's universe.

[h1]Word to the devs: It's either 'magic' hacking, or it's realistic. Pick your direction and don't try to do both at once.[/h1]

I guess my complaints kind of revolved around the fence sitting. Why go to all that trouble to get many technical details right, but still use hacking tools that so advanced as to appear 'magic' but at the same time retarded in so many easily fixed ways.

They even showed enough 'nix savvy to use tools like ps and kill mostly accurately and to cleverly make 'nmap' the command to trigger a scan for listening ports.

[b]Ironically, I guess that proves Bit's programming skills are a bit hit or miss (pun intended.)[/b] He did make nmap not require all its real-life complicated arguments and just assume you were doing an active port scan against the host you were connected to.

Those kind of professional pedantic nitpicks are why I wanted so badly to make this a negative review.

But not everyone is a professional sysadmin, and probably wouldn't have known or cared because they don't know better.

[h1]I am forced to admit, though...[/h1]
It's actually a very fun game. I applaud them for trying so hard to simulate the use of the command line where real sysadmins work. I also applaud them for at least trying to make people aware of the principles of security (or insecurity, as it were.)

I think it was worth the money. Nobody that doesn't live in my professional circles would be bothered by things like not being able to cd from one subdirectory directly to another because the GUI is so much easier and more convenient for this anyway.

If they would just have fixed the parser to accept partial wildcards and made the opposing sysadmins not complete clowns, I would have enjoyed it more.

On balance: 8/10 would be frustrated by the lack of being able to chain 'CD /logs && RM * && dc'  all over again.
